claims.text: A 44-year-old African American woman with no reported chronic illnesses, prior abdominal operations, known hernia or obesity presented with 24 hours of worsening diffuse crampy abdominal pain, persistent nausea, bilious vomiting and obstipation. ACE inhibitors had caused angioedema. She denied chest pain, dyspnea, hematochezia and urinary symptoms. Arrival temperature was 38.3 °C, pulse 112/min and saturation 98% on room air; a distended tender abdomen with guarding/rebound and a firm nonreducible right-lower abdominal-wall mass raised concern for peritonitis/strangulation. WBC was 14,900/µL with 82% neutrophils, lactate 2.4 mmol/L and trace urinary ketones; pregnancy/other urine screens were negative. Hemoglobin, hematocrit, platelets and liver tests were explicitly reported normal; the differential includes other numeric values without source-stated normality flags. Numeric electrolyte/renal values were preserved, while normal versus abnormal interpretations conflict between narrative/table caption. Imaging was deferred for emergent open exploration. A 4 cm fascial defect trapped adherent congested/ischemic omentum; bowel was viable. The hernia contents were released/reduced, nonviable omentum and hernia sac excised, and fascia closed with nonabsorbable sutures. Mesh was deferred for potential contamination/infection risk; elective reconstruction was only conditionally considered. Histology showed benign fibroadipose/fibrocollagenous tissue with congestion, hemorrhage and dilated vessels, without malignancy or necrotizing infection. The course was uncomplicated, with postoperative day 3 discharge after oral tolerance, pain control and return of bowel function. At two weeks the incision healed appropriately and normal activities resumed without new concerns or recurrent symptoms. Adhesive obstruction, internal hernia, malignancy and volvulus were lower-likelihood author-discussed differentials, not confirmed conditions.
